walkthrough:
Determine the extrema of $f(x) = p\sin^2 2x + q$ over $[0, \pi]$ (since $0 \le \sin^2 2x \le 1$ and $p, q > 0$):
$$\text{Minimum value} = p(0) + q = q$$
$$\text{Maximum value} = p(1) + q = p + q$$
$$\text{Range of } f: \quad q \le f(x) \le p + q \quad (\text{or } [q, p + q])$$

For $f(x) = p + q$, we have $\sin^2 2x = 1 \implies \sin 2x = \pm 1$.
On $0 \le 2x \le 2\pi$, $\sin 2x = 1$ at $2x = \frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\sin 2x = -1$ at $2x = \frac{3\pi}{2}$.
$$\text{Number of solutions} = 2$$

For $f(x) = q$, we have $\sin^2 2x = 0 \implies \sin 2x = 0$.
On $0 \le 2x \le 2\pi$, $\sin 2x = 0$ at $2x = 0, \pi, 2\pi$ ($x = 0, \frac{\pi}{2}, \pi$).
$$\text{Number of solutions} = 3$$

For $f(x) = \frac{1}{2}p + q$, we have $\sin^2 2x = \frac{1}{2} \implies \sin 2x = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.
In each of the four quadrants of $[0, 2\pi]$, there is exactly one solution for $2x$.
$$\text{Number of solutions} = 4$$

hints: Find four angles in radians to 3 s.f.
walkthrough:
Find the reference angle in radians:
$$\alpha = \sin^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\right) \approx 0.95532\text{ radians}$$

Determine all four solutions for $2x \in [0, 2\pi]$ and divide by $2$:
$$2x_1 = 0.95532 \implies x_1 \approx 0.478$$
$$2x_2 = \pi - 0.95532 = 2.18628 \implies x_2 \approx 1.09$$
$$2x_3 = \pi + 0.95532 = 4.09691 \implies x_3 \approx 2.05$$
$$2x_4 = 2\pi - 0.95532 = 5.32787 \implies x_4 \approx 2.66$$
$$(\text{Solutions: } x = 0.478, \quad 1.09, \quad 2.05, \quad 2.66)$$
